planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Kentucky lady's slipper is the most heat- and humidity-tolerant native Cypripedium and the best-suited species for Gulf South and mid-South woodland gardens.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, mimicking the rich floodplain and streamside hardwood forests of Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and the mid-South where it grows wild. It bears the largest flower of any native lady's slipper, with twisted, greenish-bronze lateral petals framing a huge, pale ivory-cream pouch veined in soft rose, opening in late spring and lasting for several weeks. Unlike the more cold-adapted northern Cypripedium species, Kentucky lady's slipper genuinely tolerates hot, humid Gulf Coast summers, making it the realistic choice for a shaded southern woodland garden rather than the classic pink lady's slipper of northern bogs. Never dig from the wild — populations are scattered and slow to recover — and expect several years of patient care with deep, consistently moist mulch before a nursery-grown division reaches full flowering size.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Best established in spring from nursery-grown divisions into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; October ladies' tresses blooms much later in the year than most Spiranthes, opening its tiny spiraled white flowers in fall in rich, shaded woods rather than open sunny meadows.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in the light shade of a woodland garden rather than the open, sunny meadow spot most Spiranthes prefer. October ladies' tresses is unusual among native orchids for both its late fall bloom time, from September into November, and its tendency toward self-pollination, with the tiny, spiraled white flowers often remaining nearly closed rather than opening wide to attract pollinators. It grows scattered through rich deciduous woods and shaded slopes across much of the eastern and southeastern United States, easy to overlook until its slender flower spike appears among fallen leaves in autumn. Because of its diminutive size, plant it in small groups and mark the location, since the narrow basal leaves are inconspicuous for most of the year and the plant is easily disturbed by ordinary garden work.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; lily-leaved twayblade grows in rich deciduous woods and shaded slopes across the eastern and midwestern US and depends on soil mycorrhizae, so wild-dug plants rarely survive transplant.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Lily-leaved twayblade produces two broad, shiny, ribbed basal leaves that could easily be mistaken for a small hosta, but in late spring it sends up a loose spike of unusual dusky purple-brown flowers with a wide, translucent lip, giving it a subtle, almost otherworldly charm among more familiar woodland wildflowers. It grows scattered through rich deciduous forest, floodplain woods, and shaded slopes across much of the eastern and midwestern United States, typically appearing as isolated individuals or small colonies rather than dense stands. Like most native terrestrial orchids it relies on a long-term relationship with soil fungi, so wild-collected plants almost never survive transplant; source only from specialist native orchid nurseries and avoid disturbing the soil around an established planting once it is settled.
